newsitem.title: USA: CSCE cocoa ends broadly lower on late spec selling.
newsitem.headline: CSCE cocoa ends broadly lower on late spec selling.

text.p: CSCE cocoa futures ended lower and toward the bottom of the day's range on Monday, pressured by a late-session round of speculative long liquidation, dealers said.
Turnover, however, was unimpressive, at an estimated 5,609 lots.
"It was thin all day, lackadaisical," said one trader. "There was spec liquidation, but some manufacturer buying at the lows kept it from being a total wash-out."

Benchmark September cocoa fell $17 per tonne on the day, to $1,500, after ranging between $1,527 and $1,495. Second-month December closed $18 lower, at $1,546, while the back months ended down $17 to $19.

Cocoa prices rose this morning, running up some $10 before buying momentum waned and scale-up trade selling emerged. Downward momentum accelerated after September broke through Friday's low of $1,515.

Dealers said today's weak close could weigh on sentiment on Tuesday. "It was a poor finish and I do expect it to falter further," said a trader. "It has closed near the lows four out of the last five sessions, which suggests a profound weakening. The specs may be losing heart."

Traders said the latest CFTC Commitment of Traders report released late Friday, which showed a decrease in the speculative (non-commercials and nonreportable) net long position to 19,443 lots as of July 29, was in mostly line with expectations.

While some traders said the CFTC data showed there was some more room for speculators to go long, other traders said it may have discouraged a few longs who anticipated a further reduction in the net long position of speculators.
"The CFTC report was as expected," said a trader. "But some longs were hoping it would be 3,000 to 4,000 lower than it came in."

On the charts, traders said September faced support at the day's low of $1,495, with the next levels seen at $1,480 and $1,475. On the upside, resistance was seen near the high of $1,527, followed by $1,540.
Fundamentally, traders await the next round of West African crop estimates expected later this month for direction.

Merrill Lynch analyst Judith Ganes said in her bi-weekly report released late last week that abundant rainfall in West African cocoa-growing regions and normal-to-above-normal soil moisture levels suggested preliminary Ivorian crop forecasts "might have been way too pessimistic."

"Crop forecasters now suggest that the main crop has potential to be close to or even exceed the 1995-96 record main crop of about 1 million tonnes," she said. "This would vastly reduce the potential for a sharp deficit next season and a plunge in global stocks to levels that would be considered tight."

But with the chance of a deficit next season still strong -- even with a better Ivorian crop -- Ganes said the market "should keep at somewhat higher levels than in 1996-97 when the market sank to a low of about $1,250 per tonne.
"We think the downside potential is about $1,400 basis September," Ganes said.
